newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: OECD confirms signs of Czech crown trouble-report.
newsitem.headline: OECD confirms signs of Czech crown trouble-report.

text.p: Growth of the Czech economy should slow in 1997 and remain subdued next year, while a current account deficit puts pressure on the crown, the OECD said in a report written before the central bank's May 27 floatation of the crown, and released on Thursday.
In its twice annual report on its member states, the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) noted the signals that led to the crown's late May crisis.
"GDP (gross domestic product) slowed in 1996, due to the deterioration of the foreign balance caused by disappointing export growth and continuing strong import demand," it said.

"Unemployment is low and real wages are increasing substantially faster than productivity...there was a sharp real exchange rate appreciation leading, during May (1997), to significant pressure to devalue," it added.
After the Czech National Bank abandoned its fixed exchange rate policy amid an attack on the crown, the currency dropped more than 10 percent below its previous mark/dollar peg.
The drop was followed by the government's announcement of austerity measures aiming to sharply slash public spending and public-sector wage growth in order to slow domestic demand.

The OECD said that using the crown's value on May 1 -- before it was floated -- as a basis: "Economic growth is projected to slow substantially, trade and currenct account deficits to grow and inflation to accelerate slightly, due to adjustments in still-regulated prices and VAT rates."
Without factoring in the crown's late-May drop, the OECD forecast real growth in Czech 1997 GDP of 2.6 percent, slowing to 2.0 percent next year, after 4.4 percent growth in 1996.
Exports were forecast to rise four percent this year and 3.6 percent next year, while imports were to rise 6.0 percent and 5.5 percent respectively.
The current account deficit was seen at 7.9 percent of GDP in 1997 and 8.7 percent in 1998, the OECD said.
Private consumption growth was forcast to slow to 5.0 percent from 6.0 percent last year and to 4.2 percent in 1998., while government consumption remains roughly flat.
Inflation, again before the crown's fall is factored in, was seen slowing to 7.9 percent in 1997 after 8.1 percent last year, but accelerating to 8.6 percent next year.

"The major risks relate to the strength of domestic demand, the current account deficit and confidence in the crown. Pressures on the crown have reflected tensions between the growth of real wages and productivity and these tensions persist in the projection," the OECD said.

"Unless there is either much slower real-wage growth and/or higher productivity growth, recent instability in the external accounts could intensify, which would require a further tightening of macroeconomic policy to be consistent with the present exchange rate parity," it concluded.
Economist widely expect their previous forecasts to require changes to reflect the fall of the crown.
